# The Ecology of Attention

I want to write about attention, but not in the way we usually talk about it. We tend to speak of attention as a resource: we pay attention, we spend attention, we compete for attention, we sell attention. The metaphor is almost always economic. But I have come to believe that this metaphor is not only incomplete; it is actively harmful. It turns the most intimate and vital process of being alive into a transaction. So I want to propose a different metaphor: attention as an ecology.

The word *attention* comes from the Latin *attendere*, meaning to stretch toward. It is not a coin we hand over but a reaching, a leaning in, a form of tending. In fact, *attend* and *tend* share a root. To attend to something is to tend to it, to care for it. An ecology is a web of relationships, nutrient cycles, slow decay, sudden blooms. It is not a wallet. It is not a budget. It is a living system. And like any living system, it can be rich and diverse, or it can be degraded into a monoculture.

I remember walking in a forest once, not with any particular goal, but simply moving through the trees. My attention was not fixed on one thing. It moved from the sound of a woodpecker to the pattern of light on the trail to the smell of damp earth. I was not switching tasks the way I do when I check my phone while pretending to listen to a friend. I was being held in a web of perception. The birdcall did not interrupt the light; the light did not compete with the smell. They coexisted, layered, alive. That experience felt less like focusing and more like breathing.

Modern life, by contrast, often feels like being yanked by invisible wires. Notifications, headlines, feeds, infinite scroll. The so-called attention economy treats our reaching as something to be harvested. But the problem is not only that our attention is stolen; it is that the very language we use to describe it has been colonized. When we say we are “paying” attention, we implicitly accept that attention is a finite currency to be spent on the highest bidder. In an economy, everything is fungible. One minute of attention equals any other. But in an ecology, different kinds of attention have different functions. The glance across a room at a friend, the hours-long reading of a difficult novel, the diffuse awareness of a forest, the intense focus of solving a problem—these are not interchangeable units. They are different species in the same ecosystem.

I have been thinking about boredom. We treat boredom as an emergency, a void to be filled as quickly as possible. But in an ecological metaphor, boredom is not the absence of attention; it is the fallow period. A field left fallow restores its nutrients. A mind left without external stimulation begins to produce its own connections. The modern terror of boredom is really a terror of unmediated selfhood. We reach for the phone because the alternative is encountering our own unformatted thoughts. Yet creativity emerges from that fallow soil. The first minutes of a walk without headphones can feel like a detox. Then the mind starts noticing: the way light falls on a wall, the smell of rain, a memory rising from nowhere. That shift is the ecology restoring itself.

The Australian Aboriginal songlines offer a profound example of attention as an ecology. In many Indigenous cultures, the land is not just a physical space but a mnemonic network. Attention to landscape becomes a way of remembering law, stories, ancestors. The shape of a hill is not just geography; it is a verse. A waterhole is a name. Walking through country while singing the song is a way of tending both memory and place. Here attention is not a passive reception but an active participation in a living web. We are shaped by what we repeatedly attend to. We become the ecology we inhabit. If we attend to fragmented feeds, our inner landscape becomes fragmented. If we attend to slow natural patterns, we grow into that slowness.

This is why walking has always been a technology of attention. The flâneur, the Romantic poet wandering the Lake District, the Japanese practice of *shinrin-yoku* or forest bathing—all recognize that walking without a goal allows the mind to wander in a way that is not waste but a mode of cognition. Neuroscience speaks of the default mode network, which activates during mind-wandering and is associated with creativity, self-reflection, and future planning. Aimless thought is an essential nutrient in the ecology of attention. It is not the opposite of focus; it is the soil from which focus can grow.

Writing, too, is a training in attention. To write about something is to attend to it twice: first in perception, then in language. The act of describing a tree forces you to notice its branch structure, the color of its leaves, the way it moves in the wind. Writing is not just a way of expressing what we already know; it is a way of discovering what we have not yet noticed. This essay itself is an attempt to attend to attention, to tend it. The word *essay* comes from the French *essayer*, to try. To write an essay is to try to think, to try to see, to try to care. It is a practice of attention.

But we should be careful not to romanticize deep attention at the expense of all other modes. The literary scholar N. Katherine Hayles has distinguished between deep attention—the ability to concentrate on a single object for long periods—and hyper attention, which is rapid switching, scanning, monitoring multiple streams. Both have value. The problem is not hyper attention per se but the elimination of depth. An ecosystem with only one species is fragile. A mind that can only scan is vulnerable to manipulation. We need diversity: some focused attention, some diffuse attention, some playful attention, some reverent attention. The goal is not to become a productivity machine but to be present to our own lives.

Attention and love are deeply intertwined. Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. To attend to someone is to love them. In relationships, the quality of attention we give is the quality of love we offer. When we are distracted by our phones while talking to a friend, we are saying: this moment is less valuable than the possibility of a notification. The ecology of attention includes our ethical relations. It is not just about individual focus; it is about how we care for each other. Love is not a feeling so much as a sustained act of attention. The gardener’s attention to soil moisture, to pests on leaves, to the color of new growth—that patient, repetitive, attentive care is a model for how to attend to a person, a project, a problem.

William James, the great philosopher of attention, said that the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention is the root of judgment, character, and will. He was right. But I would add that the faculty of letting attention wander is also a root of creativity, empathy, and rest. Attention is not only a discipline; it is also a release. It is the thread that stitches moments into a life. Without it, we have duration but not experience. The hours spent scrolling feel like no time at all because they are not truly attended; they are consumed. Attention is how we experience time. Deep attention stretches time; distraction makes it vanish.

The problem of information overload is often misdiagnosed. We are not overloaded with information; we are overloaded with stimuli that mimic information. True information requires integration, reflection, digestion. Attention is the digestive system of the mind. If we keep eating without digesting, we starve. The ecology metaphor reminds us that we need decomposers, not just producers. Our mental ecosystem needs time for breakdown, for turning raw experience into compost. That process is invisible and slow, often called rest, sleep, daydreaming. Without it, the soil becomes depleted.

Attention Restoration Theory, developed by Rachel and Stephen Kaplan, suggests that natural environments restore directed attention through what they call “soft fascination”: elements like clouds, leaves, water hold attention without demanding effort. They allow the directed attention system to rest. This is another reason the ecology metaphor works: our attention has different modes, and some modes restore others. A diverse attention ecosystem includes streams and forests, not just office desks and notification screens. We need places where our attention can be held without being captured.

The internet is not the enemy. It is a form of attention, and it can be rich and connective. The problem is when it becomes a monoculture. We can love Twitter and also love silence. The issue is the erosion of silence. Silence is not the absence of sound but the absence of demand. Silence is the soil where our own thoughts can germinate. Without silence, we only echo others. I once spent a week without internet. The first days were uncomfortable, restless. Then I noticed a shift: my attention felt wider, less jerky. I read a novel in two days. I remembered dreams. I wrote long letters. When I returned, the internet felt loud but also less compelling. It was not a moral victory, just an experiment in attention ecology. I realized that my attention had been like a lawn: constantly mowed, uniform, shallow. The week offline allowed it to become a meadow: unruly, diverse, humming.

Attention is also a commons. The enclosure of the commons in early capitalism parallels the enclosure of attention by digital platforms. Our inner lives are being fenced off and sold. But unlike land, attention is not a finite resource; it is a living process. We can reclaim it by practicing commoning: shared reading groups, collective silence, conversation without phones, walks with friends. The commons of attention is maintained by mutual care. It is not owned by anyone, but it must be tended by everyone.

Technology companies design for engagement, but engagement is not attention; it is often its opposite. Engagement is captured attention, but attention is also a kind of freedom. The difference is consent and agency. We can choose to give our attention; we cannot choose to be engaged. The ecology metaphor helps here: an ecosystem is not owned; it is lived in. We need to build ecosystems of attention that are not owned by anyone, that are common, diverse, self-sustaining. This requires not just individual habits but structural changes: public spaces that invite lingering, libraries and parks and benches without screens, education that trains attention rather than just testing retention.

I think often about the relationship between attention and death. Attention is the experience of being alive. The opposite of attention is not distraction but absence. To die is to cease attending. This is why we fear death: it is the end of noticing. But if we spend our lives not noticing, we are already partly absent. The practice of attention is a practice of being alive. Every act of noticing is a small defiance of death. This is not morbid; it is clarifying. It reminds us that time is made of moments, and moments are made of attention.

Art is the deliberate arrangement of attention. A painting directs the eye; a poem directs the ear; a film directs the gaze. Artists are attention ecologists: they create conditions for certain kinds of noticing. Their work trains us to see differently. This is why art is not a luxury; it is a necessary part of the attention ecosystem. It introduces diversity, challenges habits, opens new pathways. In a world saturated with algorithmic feeds, art is a form of resistance. It refuses to be optimized. It insists on its own pace, its own demands.

The pandemic taught us something important about attention. When screens became the only window, our attention became more fragile. We felt the loss of incidental attention: the glance at a stranger in a café, the shared silence of a cinema, the casual observation of a coworker’s mood. Those small attentions are part of the social ecology. Their loss was a kind of ecological collapse. Rebuilding means not just returning to normal but designing for attention diversity. We need spaces that allow for both solitude and conviviality, for both focus and drift.

I do not want to prescribe a program of attention hygiene. That would turn attention back into a productivity tool. The point is not to optimize our minds but to inhabit them more fully. It is to recognize that our attention is not a resource to be extracted but a living relationship to the world. It is to ask not “How can I get more done?” but “What deserves my attention?” and “How do I want to be shaped by what I attend to?”

Let me end with a small memory. I was sitting in a garden, doing nothing. At first, my mind was restless, reaching for a phone that was not there. Then I noticed a bee moving from flower to flower. I watched it for what felt like a long time. The bee was not efficient. It wandered, paused, doubled back. But it was attending to the flowers, and the flowers were attending to it. I do not know if that is a true ecology or just a projection. But it felt like a lesson. Attention is not a thing we have; it is a thing we share. We are not the owners of our attention; we are participants in its web.

So let us cultivate an ecology of attention. Let us plant trees of deep reading, streams of conversation, meadows of idle thought, forests of solitude. Let us resist the monoculture of the feed. Let us attend to what we love, and love what we attend to. The world is full of signals, but only attention turns them into meaning. We are the gardeners of our own minds. The harvest is not productivity but presence. And presence, in the end, is the only abundance that matters.
